title: Polymers: how lined-up chains, twists and ties decide whether a material bends, stretches or snaps

summary.text: Tear a sheet of newspaper from top to bottom, and the tear runs straight. Tear it from side to side, and the tear wanders. Pull a wisp of cotton wool and it falls apart, but twist the same wisp and it becomes a thread. Cornflour and water dry into a film that cracks when folded, until a little glycerine is added. All of these are polymers, long chains of small pieces, and what matters is how the chains are arranged and how they are held to each other. Your child tears, twists, spins and cooks to find out, and follows the idea to Kevlar, to the rice they chew, and to the proteins that every cell builds.
summary.art: A child's hands twisting a wisp of white cotton wool into a thread, beside a torn newspaper with one straight edge, with a zoom-in circle showing long chains lined up side by side.

intro.hook: Take a sheet of newspaper. Tear it from top to bottom. Now tear another sheet from side to side. One tear runs as straight as a ruler. The other wanders about. It is the same kind of paper, and you tore it the same way. So what is different?
intro.text: Paper is a mat of tiny plant fibres. When it is made, most of the fibres end up lying in one direction. A tear finds it easy to go between lined-up fibres, so it runs straight. Across them, the tear has to break fibres and wanders. In this unit you find out why lined-up fibres matter, and what the fibres are made of. You twist cotton into thread, cook a plastic-like film from cornflour, and heat plastic strips in hot water. You meet the chemist who found a fibre stronger than steel in a bowl of cloudy liquid.
intro.art: Two torn sheets of newspaper side by side, one with a long straight torn edge and one with a wavy torn edge, and a child's finger pointing at the difference.

outcomes: I can explain that a polymer is a long chain of small pieces called monomers, and give examples that living things make and examples that people make.
I can explain why short fibres, twisted together, make a long thread that is strong, even though no fibre runs from one end to the other.
I can explain why a material is stronger along the direction its chains or fibres line up in, and weaker across it.
I can explain how water, heat or a plasticiser such as glycerine loosen the holds between chains, so a material bends or stretches.
I can explain the difference between a thermoplastic and a thermoset, and name one of each.
I can run a fair test that changes one thing, repeat it, and say what the results show.
I can explain that starch and cellulose are chains of the same sugar piece, joined in different ways, and why this matters to our bodies.

terms.meaning: One small piece that can join to others to make a chain. Mono means one.
terms.example: Glucose, a sugar, is the monomer of starch and cellulose.
terms.art: A single bead on a table, with a label that says one monomer.

terms.meaning: A very long molecule made of many monomers joined in a chain. Poly means many.
terms.example: Cotton, hair, rubber and a plastic carry bag are all made of polymers.
terms.art: A long necklace of identical beads, with one bead circled.

terms.meaning: The joining of monomers, one after another, to make a polymer.
terms.example: A cotton plant joins glucose pieces into cellulose, and a factory joins ethylene pieces into polythene.
terms.art: Beads being threaded one at a time onto a growing string.

terms.meaning: A polymer made of glucose pieces joined into long straight chains. Plants build their walls and fibres from it.
terms.example: Cotton thread and paper are mostly cellulose.
terms.art: A cotton boll next to a zoom-in circle that shows straight chains lying side by side.

terms.meaning: A polymer made of the same glucose pieces as cellulose, but joined so the chains coil and branch. Plants store food as starch.
terms.example: Rice, potato and cornflour are mostly starch.
terms.art: A steel plate of rice with a zoom-in circle that shows coiled chains.

terms.meaning: A polymer made of pieces called amino acids joined in a chain. Every cell builds proteins.
terms.example: Hair, wool and silk are made of protein.
terms.art: A strand of hair beside a zoom-in circle of a folded chain of beads of many colours.

terms.meaning: A very thin, thread-like piece of material, much longer than it is wide.
terms.example: A cotton fibre is about as long as your thumb joint. A silk fibre can be hundreds of metres long.
terms.art: A single cotton fibre drawn next to a thumb for size.

terms.meaning: A long thread made by twisting fibres together.
terms.example: The thread in a sari or a cotton towel is yarn.
terms.art: A hand twisting loose fibres into a yarn, with the twist drawn as a spiral.

terms.meaning: Twisting loose fibres into a yarn.
terms.example: A takli, a charkha and a coir wheel are all used for spinning.
terms.art: A woman spinning cotton on a charkha, with thread winding onto a spindle.

terms.meaning: A small molecule that sits between polymer chains and lets them slide past each other, so the material bends more easily.
terms.example: Glycerine makes a cornflour film bend instead of crack.
terms.art: Two lines of long chains, one pressed tight together and one with small round dots between the chains.

terms.meaning: A plastic that softens when heated and hardens again when cooled, so it can be melted and shaped again.
terms.example: A polythene bag and a PET water bottle are thermoplastics.
terms.art: A plastic bottle softening in hot water, with a thermometer beside it.

terms.meaning: A plastic whose chains are tied to each other in many places during making. Once set, it does not melt again, and it burns or cracks if heated too much.
terms.example: The black handle of a pressure cooker is often a thermoset.
terms.art: A pressure cooker with a black handle, and a zoom-in circle that shows chains tied together in a net.

terms.meaning: A tie that joins one polymer chain to another.
terms.example: Sulfur makes cross-links in tyre rubber.
terms.art: Two long chains drawn side by side with short rungs between them like a ladder.

explanations.concept: How a polymer is built: monomers joined in a chain
explanations.definition: A polymer is a very long molecule made of many small pieces, called monomers, joined one after another. Making the chain is called polymerisation.
explanations.description: A chain of paper clips is a good picture. One clip is a monomer. Link thousands together and you have a polymer. In a real polymer, each link is a strong chemical bond between atoms. A polythene bag is made of ethylene monomers joined thousands of times. A PET bottle is made of two kinds of monomer, joined in turn, one kind then the other. Living things build polymers too. A cotton plant joins glucose pieces into cellulose. Every cell in your body joins amino acids into proteins, in the order written in your genes. A chain in a plastic often has ten thousand pieces or more. If each piece were a paper clip, one chain would be about three hundred metres long.
examples: Ethylene monomers joined into polythene, the plastic of a carry bag.
Amino acid monomers joined into silk, wool and hair.
Glucose monomers joined into starch in rice and cellulose in cotton.
explanations.art: A chain of paper clips, one clip circled and labelled monomer, and the whole chain labelled polymer.

explanations.concept: Same pieces, different chains: starch and cellulose
explanations.definition: Starch and cellulose are both chains of glucose. The pieces are joined in a slightly different way, so starch chains coil and cellulose chains lie straight.
explanations.description: Rice and cotton are both made of glucose chains. The difference is in the join between one glucose and the next. In starch the join makes the chain curl into a coil, and a coil is easy to pull apart. In cellulose the join keeps the chain straight, so many chains can lie side by side and hold each other tightly. That is why cotton makes a strong fibre and rice makes soft food. Your saliva and your gut have enzymes, which are tools made by cells, that cut the starch joins. When you chew rice for a while, the chains are cut into small sugars, and the rice tastes sweeter. You have no enzyme for the cellulose joins, so you cannot digest cotton. A cow can eat grass because microbes in her stomach cut cellulose for her.
examples: Chewed rice tastes sweeter because saliva cuts starch chains into small sugars.
Cotton cannot be digested by people, because we have no tool to cut cellulose.
Termites and cows depend on microbes to digest cellulose.
explanations.art: Two drawings of glucose chains: a coiled chain labelled starch, and straight chains lying side by side labelled cellulose.

explanations.concept: Lined-up chains make a material strong in one direction
explanations.definition: A material made of chains or fibres is strongest along the direction they line up in, and weakest across it.
explanations.description: Pulling along a chain pulls on strong bonds. Pulling across chains only pulls on the weak holds between neighbours. Newspaper has a grain because most of its fibres lie one way, so it tears straight along the grain. In a factory, plastics are often stretched on purpose, so that the chains line up. A stretched nylon thread is much stronger than the same nylon before it is stretched. Stephanie Kwolek found that her stiff polymer chains lined up by themselves in a liquid, and the fibre she spun was stronger than steel for the same weight. Bone and wood are the same: strong along the grain, easy to split along it.
examples: Newspaper tears straight along its grain.
Wood splits easily along the grain and is hard to snap across.
Nylon thread is stretched in the factory so the chains line up.
explanations.art: Two sheets drawn with arrows: lined-up fibres with a pull along them labelled strong, and a pull across them labelled weak.

explanations.concept: Short fibres, long thread: why twist holds
explanations.definition: A yarn is made of short fibres twisted together. Twisting presses the fibres against each other, and the grip between them holds the yarn together.
explanations.description: A cotton fibre is usually only about one to three centimetres long. A cotton thread on a spool can be hundreds of metres long. No fibre runs from one end of the thread to the other. Each fibre overlaps the ones next to it. When you pull the yarn, the fibres try to slide past each other. The twist squeezes them together, so they grip, and the harder you pull, the harder they grip. Too little twist and the fibres slide out. Too much twist and the yarn kinks and hurts itself. Silk is different. A silkworm spins one fibre hundreds of metres long, so silk needs far less twist. A rope breaks where its twist has been worn loose, because the fibres slide out.
examples: Cotton yarn: short fibres, twisted.
Coir rope: coconut fibres a hand long, twisted into a rope that holds a boat.
Silk: one very long fibre from a cocoon.
explanations.art: A cotton yarn drawn very large, showing short fibres overlapping each other in a spiral, with a pull arrow and little arrows showing the squeeze.

explanations.concept: Water, heat and plasticisers loosen the holds between chains
explanations.definition: Chains in a material are held to each other by weak ties. Water, heat or a plasticiser such as glycerine loosen the ties, so the chains slide and the material bends.
explanations.description: In hair, wool and cotton, chains are held side by side by weak ties called hydrogen bonds. Water gets between the chains and loosens the ties. That is why a curl stretches when wet. In a dry cornflour film, the starch chains stick tightly to each other, so the film is stiff and cracks when you fold it. Glycerine is a small molecule that sits between the chains and keeps them a little apart. Now the chains can slide, and the film bends. Heat does the same thing. Warm chains wiggle more, and holds between them break and form again. That is why a thermoplastic softens in heat. Plastic makers add a lot of plasticiser to PVC to make soft hose, and leave it out to make stiff pipe.
examples: A wet curl stretches and springs back when dry.
Glycerine turns a stiff starch film into a bendy one.
A soft PVC garden hose has plasticiser added, and a stiff PVC pipe is the same polymer without it.
explanations.art: Two drawings of chains: tight together labelled stiff, and with small dots between them labelled bendy.

explanations.concept: Thermoplastics and thermosets: tied loosely or tied everywhere
explanations.definition: A thermoplastic has chains that are free to slide when heated, so it softens and can be shaped again. A thermoset has chains tied to each other in many places, so it does not melt.
explanations.description: A thermoplastic is like a bowl of cooked noodles. Warm it and the noodles slide. Cool it and they hold their new shape. Polythene, PET and polystyrene are thermoplastics, and so they can be melted and recycled. A thermoset is like a fishing net. The strands are tied at every crossing, so heat cannot make them slide. Leo Baekeland made the first fully man-made plastic, Bakelite, in 1907, and it was a thermoset. Pressure cooker handles are often made of a similar kind of plastic, because they must not soften on the stove. A thermoset cannot be melted and moulded again. Heated too much, it chars. Tyre rubber is a lightly tied thermoset. Ties placed here and there keep it stretchy, and many ties make it hard.
examples: A PET bottle is a thermoplastic and can be melted and reshaped.
A black pressure cooker handle is a thermoset and does not soften on the stove.
Tyre rubber is tied by cross-links made with sulfur.
explanations.art: Left: noodle-like chains sliding past each other in heat. Right: chains tied at many points into a net, with a flame beneath that does not loosen it.

explanations.concept: Is a pressure cooker handle one giant molecule?
explanations.description: In a thermoset, the strong ties run through the whole piece. Every atom is joined to the others by strong bonds. If you trace a path along the bonds, you can reach almost any atom from any other. So some chemists say that a thermoset handle is one single giant molecule. Others say that a molecule is a particular group of atoms with a particular size, and a net of unknown size is not one. Nobody has to settle this to use the handle, but it shows how a word like molecule gets stretched when we look closely.
examples: A cooker handle made of a thermoset.
A vulcanised rubber band, where chains are tied together in a loose net.

perspectives.explanation: Yes. All the atoms are joined by strong bonds into one connected piece, so it is one giant molecule.
No. A molecule means a group of atoms with a set size and shape. A net that could be any size is a network, not a molecule.

explanations.art: A black cooker handle with a zoom-in circle showing a net of tied chains, and a question mark over it.

agreed.text: Plastics, rubber, cotton, silk, wool, hair and starch are all polymers: long chains of small pieces joined end to end.
agreed.evidence: Chemists can measure the length of chains and can join monomers into chains in the lab, as Wallace Carothers did when he made nylon in the 1930s.

agreed.text: Starch and cellulose are made of the same sugar, glucose, joined in different ways.
agreed.evidence: The shapes of both molecules have been worked out by X-rays and chemistry, and enzymes that cut starch do not cut cellulose.

agreed.text: A material made of chains is strongest along the direction the chains are lined up in.
agreed.evidence: Paper tears straight along its grain, wood splits along its grain, and nylon and polythene become stronger when they are stretched in the factory.

agreed.text: Twisting short fibres together holds them in a yarn, because the twist makes the fibres grip each other.
agreed.evidence: Yarn made of fibres of a few centimetres can be hundreds of metres long, and a yarn untwisted comes apart into loose fibres.

agreed.text: A thermoplastic softens in heat and can be reshaped, and a thermoset does not.
agreed.evidence: Bottles can be melted and recycled, while Bakelite and similar plastics burn or crack when heated too much.

challenging.claim: A long, strong thread must have long, strong fibres that run from one end to the other.
challenging.for: A rope looks like it must be made of fibres as long as the rope.
challenging.against: Cotton fibres are one to three centimetres long, and cotton yarn can be hundreds of metres long. Twist makes the short fibres grip each other.

challenging.claim: Pulling on a plastic only damages it.
challenging.for: A plastic bag stretches and then tears.
challenging.against: Makers stretch nylon and polythene on purpose, because stretching lines up the chains and makes the plastic stronger along the stretch.

challenging.claim: Natural materials are always better than plastics.
challenging.for: Cotton, wood and paper can rot back into soil, and plastic bags can stay in the environment for a very long time.
challenging.against: Cotton needs a lot of water to grow. Some people are allergic to natural rubber. Plastic keeps hospitals clean and food fresh. Natural and made are not the same as good and bad.

challenging.claim: A plastic sold as biodegradable breaks down quickly wherever it ends up.
challenging.for: Some plastics do break down in a compost heap that is kept hot.
challenging.against: In one study, some bags sold as biodegradable could still carry shopping after three years in soil. How fast a plastic breaks down depends on where it is.

challenging.claim: A stronger chemical bond always means a stronger material.
challenging.for: Strong bonds hold the atoms of a chain together.
challenging.against: A cotton thread, a tyre and a spider's silk are held together by the holds between chains and fibres. How chains are arranged and tied matters as much as the strength of a bond.

big_questions.q: No fibre in a cotton thread runs from one end to the other. So what makes the thread one thing?
big_questions.hint: Think about what happens to the fibres when you pull, and what the twist does.

big_questions.q: Starch and cellulose are chains of the same sugar. Why can you digest rice but not cotton?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the chewing of rice does, and what tool would be needed to cut a straight chain.

big_questions.q: A pressure cooker handle has strong ties through all of it. Is it one giant molecule, or many?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you mean by one thing, and what you would count if you tried to count its molecules.

big_questions.q: Plastic is made from oil, and most oil formed from tiny sea creatures that lived millions of years ago. In what way is a plastic bottle very old life?
big_questions.hint: Think about where the atoms in the chains were before they were in the bottle.

big_questions.q: The finest cloth in old Bengal was spun by hand, mostly by women, into thread so fine that it almost could not be seen. Who gets remembered for the things we wear?
big_questions.hint: Think about the people who grow, spin, weave and sew the clothes you wear today.

story.title: The Rope That Came Apart
story.note: A made-up story. Coir spinning near Alappuzha in Kerala is real, and it is mostly done by women. The coir fibres, the twist that holds them, and a rope wearing out where it rubs are all real. Anitha, her family and the storm are imagined.
text: Anitha lived beside a canal near Alappuzha, in Kerala, where the backwaters wind between coconut palms. At the bottom of her steps, a small wooden boat called a vallam was tied to a post. Her grandmother, Ammumma, spun coir for a living, as many women in the village did.
In the monsoon, a storm came in the night. The wind pushed the palms flat, and the canal heaved. In the morning, the post stood empty. The rope was gone, and so was the vallam.
Her uncle Shaji found the boat two hours later. It was stuck in the reeds at the edge of a paddy field, dented but whole. He carried the rope home in his hand, and held up the broken end.
'Old rope,' he said. 'It was bound to go one day.'

Anitha took the broken end to the veranda. It did not end in a neat cut. It ended in a brown brush of rough hairs. She pulled one out and held it in front of her face. It was as long as her hand. She pulled it between her fingers, and it snapped.
'How can this hold a boat?' she said. 'One hair breaks if I just pull.'
Ammumma was sitting at her spinning wheel. 'Come here, and I will show you,' she said.
She took a handful of loose coconut husk fibres and laid them in a line on Anitha's palm. 'Pull,' she said. Anitha pulled one end. The fibres slid apart like hair coming out of a comb.

Then Ammumma hooked a few fibres to the wheel. She turned the handle with one hand, and walked backwards, feeding more fibres with the other. A thin brown thread grew out of her fingers. It grew longer, and longer, until it reached the far wall of the veranda.
'Now pull,' she said.
Anitha pulled the thread. It did not come apart. She pulled harder. It held.
'It is only twist,' said Ammumma. 'The twist squeezes the fibres together. Each one grips its neighbours. And the harder you pull, the harder they grip.'
Anitha looked at the long thread, and at the tiny hairs in her hand. 'But the thread is as long as the wall, and each fibre is only as long as my hand. Where does one fibre go?'

'It stops,' said Ammumma, 'and another starts next to it. No single fibre goes the whole way. They are all short, and they hold each other.' She smiled. 'A rope is not one long thing. It is a great many short things that hold on.'
Anitha ran her thumb along the broken rope. Near the break, the rope was smooth and shiny. Further along, it was rough and tight. She frowned, and called her uncle.
'Uncle Shaji, where did the rope touch the step?'
He thought. 'It rubbed on the stone, right there, all season.'

'Look.' She held up the shiny part. 'The twist is loose here. The fibres have been rubbed until they slide.' She pulled one fibre out of the shiny part, and it slid out easily. Then she tried the same on the rough part, and the fibre would not move. 'The fibres did not break. They slid out. The rope did not fail where it was weak. It failed where the holding was gone.'
Uncle Shaji looked at the rope for a long time. Then he laughed. 'My niece is teaching me about rope.'
'Ammumma taught me,' said Anitha.

That afternoon, the three of them fixed it. Uncle Shaji cut off the worn end and tied the new end to the post. Anitha wrapped an old sack around the place where the rope would touch the stone step. Ammumma checked every handspan of the rope with her fingers, pressing to feel any place where the twist was loose.

At school, Anitha's teacher had told her that every plant fibre is made of chains of tiny pieces, too small to see. Anitha thought about that on the veranda. Chains twisted into fibres. Fibres twisted into yarn. Yarn twisted into strands. Strands twisted into a rope. At every size, the holding was done by pieces that were short, and gripped the ones beside them.
The next storm came a week later. Anitha stood on the steps with a torch. The wind pulled at the vallam, and the vallam pulled at the rope. The rope went tight, and it held.
'It is only twist,' said Anitha, to nobody. And she went in to dry her hair.
story.epiphany: For the parent: a rope, a cotton thread and a yarn are made of short fibres that overlap. Twist makes them grip each other, so the thread is longer and stronger than any fibre in it. A rope fails where the twist is worn loose, because the fibres slide out, rather than because the fibres break.
ask: Why did Anitha's one fibre snap, but the whole thread hold?
Where did the rope fail, and why did it fail there?
No fibre runs the whole length of the rope. So how can the rope be one strong thing?
What do you think would have happened if Ammumma had not twisted the fibres?

games.title: Chain Detectives: natural polymer, made polymer or not a polymer?

printables.title: 12 tokens: four that say Natural polymer, four that say Made polymer and four that say Not a polymer

rules: One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader does not show the back.
Every other player puts one token face down. Then everyone turns the tokens over together.
The reader reads the back. Every player whose token matches the first words of the back scores one point.
A player who also says one thing about how the material behaves, for example that it stretches, bends or does not melt, scores one more point. The reader decides, using the back of the card.
With two players, the parent and the child swap the reader's job after every card. With one player, read the front, choose a token, then check the back and keep your own score.
After each card, the reader's job passes to the player on the left.
The game ends when all 24 cards have been read. The player with the most points wins. If there is a tie, the tied players share the win.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards and the 12 tokens. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile. Give each player one token of each kind.
flow.say: These cards show things around us. Each player gets three tokens. Natural polymer, made polymer and not a polymer. We will guess what each thing is.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Take three tokens.
flow.context: This is the first step of Chain Detectives. You set up the cards and the tokens.

flow.do: Play the first six cards. After each card, read the back aloud. After card three, ask the question below.
flow.say: The reader reads the front. Everyone else chooses a token. Turn the tokens over together. Now the reader reads the back. Who scored? Who can say more?
flow.kid: The reader reads a card. Pick a token. Turn it over. Check the back.

ask.q: What do the polymers on these cards have in common?
good: They are made of small pieces joined together.
They have a monomer that repeats.

flow.context: In this step, you play the first six cards and learn how to score.

flow.do: Play the next eight cards. Swap the reader's job after every card. Keep a tally of points on paper.
flow.say: Keep going. Ask yourself two things. Is it made of long chains of one small piece? Did a living being make it, or a factory?
flow.kid: Play on. Is it a long chain? Who made it?

ask.q: Which card surprised you so far, and why?
good: Hair and plastic are the same kind of thing.
Salt and sugar are not polymers.

flow.context: In this step, you play the middle of the game and keep score.

flow.do: Play the last ten cards. When the pile is finished, count each player's points.
flow.say: Last cards. Think about chains. Where are the long chains in this thing, and what makes them?
flow.kid: Play the last cards. Count your points.
flow.context: In this step, you finish the pile and count the points.

flow.do: Say who won. Ask your child which card was the hardest to place, and why.
flow.say: Who got the most points? Which card was hardest? Why was it hard?
flow.kid: Who won? Which card was hardest? Why?
flow.think: Why is a hair more like a plastic bag than like a sugar crystal?
flow.context: This is the last step of Chain Detectives. You look back at the game.

experiments.title: Cornflour Film: what does glycerine do?
experiments.question: Three films are cooked from the same cornflour mix, with none, one or two teaspoons of glycerine. Which film bends the most before it cracks?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which film will fold the most times before it cracks, and which will crack first? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All three films start from one pot of the same mix. Each gets the same amount, spread to the same size and thickness, and dried in the same place for the same time. Only the amount of glycerine changes. The film with no glycerine is the control. Each film is folded twice, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: 3 level tablespoons of cornflour (corn starch)
12 tablespoons of water, about 180 millilitres
3 teaspoons of vinegar
3 teaspoons of glycerine, from a chemist shop
a small steel pan and a spoon, and a stove
3 small steel katoris, and 3 steel plates or 3 pieces of foil
a few drops of cooking oil, a ruler and a marker pen
the results table and a pencil

experiments.safety: An adult does the cooking. The mix gets hot and sticky, like hot custard, so keep children back from the stove. Do not taste the films.

schedule.what: Cook the mix, add the glycerine and pour three films.
Peel the films. Fold them, stretch them and draw the chart.

experiments.record: For each film, write the glycerine amount, the number of folds before it cracked on each try, and how far it stretched. Draw a bar chart with one bar for each film. Write three lines: what I thought, what I saw, and why.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you cook a plastic-like film from cornflour and test how the amount of glycerine changes how the film bends.

setup.art: A pan on a stove with white cornflour and water being stirred, and a steel spoon.
setup.caption: 1. An adult stirs cornflour, water and vinegar on low heat until the mix turns clear and thick.

setup.art: Three small steel katoris of clear gel in a row, labelled 0, 1 and 2, with a teaspoon pouring glycerine into the third.
setup.caption: 2. Share the mix in three katoris. Add 0, 1 and 2 teaspoons of glycerine.

setup.art: Three steel plates, each with a flat circle of clear gel about 10 centimetres wide, labelled 0, 1 and 2.
setup.caption: 3. Pour and spread each one into a circle. Leave them to dry for two to four days.

setup.art: A child's hands folding a dry strip of film in half, with a count of folds written beside it.
setup.caption: 4. Cut a strip from each dry film. Fold and open it again and again, and count the folds until it cracks.

setup.art: A child pulling a short strip with two dots 5 centimetres apart and a ruler beside it.
setup.caption: 5. Pull a strip slowly and measure how far the dots move before it tears.

flow.do: Show your child the cornflour, the vinegar and the glycerine. Say you will make three films with none, one and two teaspoons of glycerine. Write down their guess and reason.
flow.say: We will cook three films from the same cornflour. One gets no glycerine. One gets one teaspoon. One gets two teaspoons. Which will fold the most times before it cracks? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: We make three films. Each has different glycerine. Which bends best? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that film will bend the most?
good: The glycerine gets between the starch.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write each guess and reason at the top of the results table. Glycerine is sold at chemist shops, often as glycerin.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Cornflour Film test. You guess before you cook.

flow.do: Put 3 tablespoons of cornflour, 12 tablespoons of water and 3 teaspoons of vinegar in the pan. Stir until no lumps remain. Then an adult heats it on low and stirs all the time.
flow.say: Stir the mix until it is smooth. An adult heats it on low and stirs all the time. After about four minutes it turns clear and thick, like custard. Then switch off the heat.
flow.kid: Stir the mix in the pan. A grown-up heats it and stirs.
flow.parent: Do not leave the pan. If it is still milky after five minutes, keep stirring a little longer. If lumps form, beat quickly with a fork. Let it cool for two minutes before the next step. The mix is hot and sticky, like hot custard.

check.q: Why do we cook the mix before we make the films?
options: Heat makes the starch swell with water, and the mix becomes a clear gel
Heat takes all the water out of the cornflour
Heat turns the cornflour into glycerine
check.why: Cornflour is starch. In hot water the starch grains swell and the chains spread out into a thick gel. If you spread cold cornflour and water, you would only get a chalky powder.

flow.context: In this step, you cook the cornflour mix that all three films will be made from.

flow.do: Spoon the hot mix into three small steel katoris, the same amount in each. Stir 1 teaspoon of glycerine into the second katori, and 2 teaspoons into the third. Add none to the first. Label them 0, 1 and 2.
flow.say: The three katoris have the same mix. The first gets no glycerine. The second gets one teaspoon. The third gets two. Stir each well. Label them.
flow.kid: Share the mix in three katoris. Add glycerine to two. Label them.
flow.parent: Use the same spoon each time and level spoonfuls. The mix is still warm, so a grown-up should help.
flow.context: In this step, you share the mix and add different amounts of glycerine.

flow.do: Rub a few drops of oil on three steel plates or three pieces of foil. Pour one katori onto each. Spread it with the back of a spoon into a circle about 10 centimetres wide and as thick as a coin.
flow.say: Pour each katori onto its own plate. Spread it into a circle the same size. Make all three the same thickness. Write 0, 1 and 2 beside them.
flow.kid: Pour each katori onto a plate. Spread it flat. Write the labels.
flow.parent: A thick film takes longer to dry and may stay sticky in the middle. Aim for about 2 to 3 millimetres.

check.q: Why must all three films be the same size and thickness?
options: So only the glycerine is different
So they look the same
So they dry faster
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If one film were much thicker, you could not tell whether glycerine or thickness made the difference.

flow.context: In this step, you spread the three films. They must all be the same size and thickness.

flow.do: Put the plates on a flat shelf where nobody will knock them. Leave them for two to four days, out of the rain. A fan helps in damp weather.
flow.say: Now we wait. The water must leave the films. Check the day after tomorrow. They are ready when they are dry and peel off easily.
flow.kid: Leave the plates on a shelf. Wait two to four days.
flow.parent: In the monsoon, drying can take longer. Do not use the oven or the sun's full heat, because the film can curl or bubble. If a film is still wet after five days, turn it over and let the other side dry.
flow.context: In this step, you leave the films to dry. This takes a few days.

flow.do: Peel each film from its plate. Look at each film and feel it. Write what each film is like, using the words stiff, bendy, sticky, clear or cloudy.
flow.say: Peel the film off the plate. Which comes off in one piece? Which feels stiff? Which feels sticky or soft? What do you notice?
flow.kid: Peel the films off. Look and feel. Write what you notice.

ask.q: How is the film with no glycerine different from the film with two teaspoons?
good: The last is softer or sticky.

flow.parent: The film with no glycerine is often stiff and may crack as you peel it. That is a result, not a mistake. The film with two teaspoons may stay a little sticky.
flow.context: In this step, you look at each dry film before testing it.

flow.do: Cut a strip 2 centimetres wide from each film. Fold the strip in half and open it again. That is one fold. Count the folds until it cracks. Stop at 20. Do each film twice.
flow.say: Fold the strip in half, then open it. That is one fold. Count every fold. Stop when it cracks, or at twenty. Do it twice for each film.
flow.kid: Fold and open a strip. Count the folds. Stop when it cracks.
flow.parent: Fold the same way each time, across the middle of the strip. Cut strips from the middle of the film, since the edges are thinner.

check.q: Film 1 cracks after 3 folds and film 2 cracks after 4 folds on one try, but after 12 folds on the next. What should you do?
options: Test again, and trust the pattern after several tries
Throw away the lowest number
Decide film 2 is magic
check.why: One try can be a fluke. When two tries differ a lot, repeat the test and look for the pattern. That is why we do each film twice or more.

flow.context: In this step, you fold each film again and again to see how much bending it can take.

flow.do: Mark two dots 5 centimetres apart on a strip. Hold the strip by its ends and pull slowly. Measure the distance between the dots when it tears.
flow.say: Make two dots five centimetres apart on a strip. Pull slowly until it tears. Measure the dots. How far did it stretch?
flow.kid: Mark dots on a strip. Pull slowly. Measure the dots.
flow.parent: A very stiff film may not stretch at all. Write 5 for no stretch. The film with the most glycerine may stretch the most, or may tear more easily because it is soft.
flow.context: In this step, you test how far each film stretches before it tears.

flow.do: Draw a bar chart of the folds for each film. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each film. Say what you thought, saw and why.
flow.parent: A strong answer says the film with no glycerine cracked first, and that the glycerine let the starch chains slide past each other. After they have said what they saw, explain: starch chains in a dry film stick tightly to each other, so the film is stiff. Glycerine molecules are small and sit between the chains and keep them a little apart. Now the chains can slide, and the film bends. Too much glycerine leaves the film soft and sticky. If your results are not in this order, write them down as they are and ask why. Films from damp weather, or a thick film, often behave differently.
flow.think: What do you think the glycerine is doing between the starch chains?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Cornflour Film test. You draw the chart and explain what you found.

experiments.title: Hot Water Plastics: what does heat do to different plastics?
experiments.question: When strips of different plastics sit in very hot water for one minute, which ones change, and how?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which strip will change the most in the hot water, and what will it do? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every strip is cut to the same size, 8 centimetres by 2 centimetres. Every strip sits in the same hot water for the same time, one minute. Only the kind of plastic changes. Measuring each strip before and after shows how much it changed.
results_table: How it looked and felt after

materials.item: four strips, each 8 centimetres by 2 centimetres, cut from a clear PET bottle, a thin carry bag, a washed milk packet and a hard plastic tub
a kettle, and about 1 litre of just-boiled water
a steel bowl, steel tongs and a steel plate
a ruler, a marker pen, scissors and a timer
the results table and a pencil

experiments.safety: An adult does all the hot-water steps. Keep the kettle and bowl away from the edge of the table. The steel bowl gets hot too, so do not touch it. Cut edges of hard plastic can be sharp.

schedule.what: Cut and measure the strips. Heat them in hot water. Measure again and explain.

experiments.record: Write the length of each strip before and after, and what it looked like. Draw a bar chart of how much each strip shrank. Write three lines: what I thought, what I saw, and why.
experiments.context: In this experiment, a grown-up heats strips of different plastics in hot water. You find out which plastics change, and what that tells us about their chains.

setup.art: Four numbered plastic strips lined up beside a ruler: a bottle strip, a carry bag strip, a milk packet strip and a hard tub strip.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cuts four strips of the same size. Number and measure them.

setup.art: A kettle pouring hot water into a steel bowl on a flat table, with a child standing back.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up pours very hot water into a steel bowl.

setup.art: Steel tongs dropping four strips into the bowl, with a timer showing one minute.
setup.caption: 3. Drop in all four strips with the tongs. Time one minute.

setup.art: Four strips on a steel plate after heating, one curled up tight, one shorter, and one unchanged, with a ruler beside them.
setup.caption: 4. Lift the strips out. When they are cool, measure and feel each one.

flow.do: Show your child the plastic things and the kettle. Say you will drop strips of different plastics into hot water. Write down their guess and reason.
flow.say: We will cut strips from four plastic things and put them in very hot water. Which strip will change the most? What will it do? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: We put plastic strips in hot water. Which changes most? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that plastic will change the most?

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write each guess and reason down. Children often guess the thinnest plastic changes most.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Hot Water test. You guess before you heat anything.

flow.do: An adult cuts four strips from a clear PET bottle, a carry bag, a milk packet and a hard plastic tub. Each strip is 8 centimetres by 2 centimetres. Number each strip with a marker. Measure each one.
flow.say: A grown-up cuts the strips. Number them one to four. Measure each strip and write its length in the table.
flow.kid: Number the strips. Measure each one. Write the length.
flow.parent: Cut the bottle strip from the straight wall, not the neck. Cut edges of hard plastic can be sharp, so round the corners. Wash the strips first.

check.q: Why do we measure each strip before it goes into the water?
options: So we can tell how much it changed
So the strips are clean
So the water boils faster
check.why: A change only means something compared with the start. Without the first length, we could not say whether a strip shrank.

flow.context: In this step, you cut and measure the strips before heating them.

flow.do: An adult boils a kettle and waits for one minute. Then the adult pours about 1 litre of the hot water into a steel bowl. Everyone else stays back.
flow.say: A grown-up boils the water and waits one minute. Then the grown-up pours it into the steel bowl. This water is dangerously hot.
flow.kid: A grown-up pours hot water into a bowl. Stand back.
flow.parent: Use a steady bowl on a flat table. Keep the kettle away from children. Do not use the microwave.
flow.context: In this step, a grown-up prepares the hot water.

flow.do: An adult drops all four strips into the water with steel tongs. Start a timer for one minute. Then the adult lifts the strips out with the tongs onto a steel plate.
flow.say: Drop all four strips in together. Watch them for one minute. What do you see happening? Then lift them out with the tongs.
flow.kid: A grown-up drops in the strips. Watch for one minute.

ask.q: What do you see the strips doing in the water?

flow.parent: Let the strips cool on the plate for a minute before touching them. Some strips may curl up quickly. Others may stay flat.
flow.context: In this step, the strips sit in hot water for one minute while you watch.

flow.do: When the strips are cool, measure each one again. Feel each one. Write the new length, and write if it is bent, limp, stiff or the same.
flow.say: Measure each strip again. Which got shorter? Which curled? Which stayed the same? How does each feel now?
flow.kid: Measure each strip again. How did each change?
flow.parent: The bottle strip and the thin bag often shrink or curl. The hard tub often stays the same. If nothing changed, the water was too cool, so re-boil and use it at once. Write what you see.
flow.context: In this step, you find out what the hot water did to each plastic.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: After they have said what they saw, explain: a bottle wall and a plastic bag are stretched when they are made, so the chains are pulled straight and lined up. In hot water the chains wiggle and coil up again, and the strip shrinks. A thick tub that was moulded, not stretched, has chains that were never pulled straight, so it hardly changes. These plastics are thermoplastics. Heat lets their chains slide.
flow.think: Why might a bottle that was stretched when it was made shrink in hot water?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Hot Water test. You explain what you found.

activities.title: Tear the Newspaper: which way does it tear straight?

materials.item: 4 sheets of old newspaper, any kind
a marker pen
a ruler
a page from an old notebook and a page from a magazine

schedule.what: Tear strips both ways, mark the straight direction, and look at the torn edge.

activities.record: Draw the sheet with an arrow showing the direction that tore straight. Write one line about why you think it tears that way.
activities.context: In this activity, you tear newspaper in two directions and find out that paper has a grain, like wood.

setup.art: A sheet of newspaper laid flat, with a thumb and finger starting a tear at the top edge, tearing downwards.
setup.caption: 1. Tear a strip from top to bottom, slowly, about 5 centimetres from the edge.

setup.art: A second sheet of newspaper with a tear starting at the side and going across.
setup.caption: 2. Tear a strip from side to side in the same way.

setup.art: The two torn edges side by side, one long and straight and one short and wavy, with an arrow drawn on the sheet along the straight one.
setup.caption: 3. Mark an arrow in the direction that tore straight.

flow.do: Give your child a sheet of newspaper. Ask them to guess which way it will tear straight, and why. Write down the guess.
flow.say: Here is a sheet of newspaper. If we tear it from top to bottom, and then from side to side, will the two tears look the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Will paper tear the same both ways? Why?

ask.q: Why might one way be straighter?
good: Something in the paper goes one way.
I do not know, let us try.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of Tear the Newspaper. You guess first.

flow.do: Tear three strips from top to bottom, slowly. Tear three more strips from side to side, slowly. Lay the torn strips in two rows.
flow.say: Tear slowly, about five centimetres from the edge. Do three strips from top to bottom. Then three strips from side to side. Lay them out in two rows.
flow.kid: Tear three strips top to bottom. Tear three strips side to side.

ask.q: What do you notice about the two rows?

flow.parent: One direction usually tears in a long straight line. The other goes wavy, or stops short. Which direction is straight depends on the paper.
flow.context: In this step, you tear the paper in two directions.

flow.do: Draw an arrow on the sheet along the direction that tore straight. Try a notebook page and a magazine page the same way. Mark the straight direction on each.
flow.say: Mark the straight direction with an arrow. Now do the same with the notebook page and the magazine page. Is the straight direction the same?
flow.kid: Draw an arrow on the straight way. Try a notebook page.
flow.parent: If both ways look alike on one sheet, try another sheet. A few papers show it less clearly. Some pages tear straight the same way, and some do not.

check.q: Both rows tore with a wavy edge on one page. What should you do?
options: Try another sheet and look for the pattern
Decide the paper has no grain
Tear much faster
check.why: A single odd result could be a fluke or a bad sheet. Test another sheet before deciding.

flow.context: In this step, you mark the straight direction and test two other papers.

flow.do: Hold a torn edge up to a window. Look for tiny hairs sticking out. Ask your child what the hairs could be.
flow.say: Hold the torn edge up to the light. What do you see sticking out? What could those tiny hairs be?
flow.kid: Look at the torn edge. What are the tiny hairs?

ask.q: What could those tiny hairs be?

flow.parent: Paper is a mat of plant fibres, pressed flat. A tear follows between the fibres where they line up, and runs ragged where it must cut across them.
flow.context: In this step, you look closely at the torn edge.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw, and why. Then say the answer yourself.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it tore straight one way?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, saw and why.
flow.parent: After they have said what they saw, explain: when paper is made, most of the fibres end up lying one way. A tear runs easily along lined-up fibres. Across them, the tear must break fibres, so it wanders. Material made of long pieces is stronger along them.
flow.think: If paper has a grain like wood, which way would it be stronger?
flow.context: This is the last step of Tear the Newspaper. You explain what you found.

activities.title: Wisp and Thread: how does twisting make cotton hold?

materials.item: a roll or packet of cotton wool
2 pencils
a ruler

schedule.what: Pull a loose wisp, twist another, and measure one fibre.

activities.record: Draw the loose wisp and the twisted thread side by side. Write how long one fibre was, and what the twist did.
activities.context: In this activity, you pull a loose wisp of cotton wool and a twisted one, and find out what twisting does to short fibres.

setup.art: Two hands holding a loose wisp of cotton wool about 15 centimetres long, pulling it slowly until it comes apart.
setup.caption: 1. Pull a loose wisp slowly. Watch what happens.

setup.art: A pencil with a wisp wrapped around its tip and a child spinning the pencil while the other hand holds the far end.
setup.caption: 2. Wrap another wisp around a pencil. Spin the pencil 30 times, the same way each time.

setup.art: The twisted thread pulled tight between two hands, and a single loose fibre laid beside a ruler.
setup.caption: 3. Pull the twisted thread. Then untwist it and measure one fibre.

flow.do: Show your child a roll of cotton wool. Pull a wisp about 15 centimetres long and as thick as a pencil. Ask them to guess what will happen if you pull it from both ends, and why.
flow.say: This is cotton wool. If I hold a wisp at both ends and pull slowly, what will happen? Now, if I twist it first, what will happen? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Pull a wisp. What will happen? What if we twist it first? Why?

ask.q: Why might twisting change what happens?

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of Wisp and Thread. You guess first.

flow.do: Pull a loose wisp about 15 centimetres long. Hold one end in each hand, 10 centimetres apart. Pull slowly. Watch what happens to the fibres.
flow.say: Hold the wisp at both ends. Pull slowly. What do the fibres do? How much pull did it take?
flow.kid: Pull a loose wisp slowly. What do the fibres do?
flow.parent: A loose wisp comes apart almost at once, the fibres sliding past each other. That is the control.
flow.context: In this step, you pull a wisp with no twist.

flow.do: Wrap one end of a new wisp round a pencil. Hold the far end between two fingers, 10 centimetres away. Spin the pencil 30 times, the same way each time. Then pull slowly.
flow.say: Wrap a new wisp round a pencil. Hold the other end with your fingers. Spin the pencil thirty times, always the same way. Now pull slowly. What is different?
flow.kid: Spin the pencil 30 times. Then pull slowly. What is different?
flow.parent: Hold the far end firmly while you spin, or the twist runs out. Keep a gentle pull on the wisp as you spin. Thirty turns should make a rough thread. It holds more than the loose wisp did.

check.q: What do the fibres do when you pull the twisted thread?
options: They grip each other and the thread holds
They slide apart, just as before
They turn into one long fibre
check.why: Twisting presses the fibres against each other. They overlap, so when you pull, they grip. If you saw no difference, add more turns.

flow.context: In this step, you twist a wisp into a thread and pull it.

flow.do: Make a third wisp. Spin the pencil 100 times. Hold the thread tight, then let the far end go. Watch what the thread does.
flow.say: Now spin a third wisp one hundred times. Let go of the far end. What does the thread do? Is more twist always better?
flow.kid: Spin 100 times. Let go. What does the thread do?

ask.q: Do you think more twist is always better?

flow.parent: With too much twist the thread curls into loops and kinks when you let go. A thread needs enough twist to grip, and not so much that it fights itself.
flow.context: In this step, you test what happens if you add far too much twist.

flow.do: Untwist the thread. Pull one fibre out with your fingers. Lay it beside a ruler and measure it. Ask your child how long the whole thread was, and how long one fibre is.
flow.say: Untwist the thread. Pull out one single fibre. Measure it. How long is one fibre? How long was the thread? Does any fibre go the whole way?
flow.kid: Pull out one fibre. Measure it. Is it as long as the thread?
flow.parent: Cotton fibres are about 1 to 3 centimetres long. The thread is many times longer. After they have said what they saw, explain: the fibres overlap, and the twist makes them grip.
flow.think: If no fibre goes the whole way, what holds the thread together?
flow.context: In this step, you measure one fibre and compare it with the thread.

activities.title: Chew the Rice: what does your mouth do to starch?

materials.item: a spoonful of plain cooked rice, or a piece of plain idli
a clock or phone timer
a glass of water

schedule.what: Chew plain rice for two minutes, and notice the taste each half minute.

activities.record: Write what the rice tasted like at the start, after 1 minute and after 2 minutes.
activities.context: In this activity, you chew a little plain rice for two minutes and notice what happens to the taste, to find out what your saliva does to starch.

setup.art: A spoonful of plain white rice on a steel plate, and a timer beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Take a small spoonful of plain rice. Taste it.

setup.art: A child chewing slowly with a timer showing one minute.
setup.caption: 2. Chew slowly. Do not swallow yet. Notice the taste each half minute.

setup.art: A child writing three lines beside a clock: start, one minute, two minutes.
setup.caption: 3. Write down what the rice tastes like at each time.

flow.do: Give your child a small spoonful of plain rice. Ask what taste they expect after two minutes of chewing, and why. Write down the guess.
flow.say: Rice does not taste of much. If you chew it for a long time, will the taste change? How? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Will rice taste different after chewing a long time? Why?

good: The mouth does something to it.

flow.parent: Use food your child already eats and is not allergic to. Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of Chew the Rice. You guess first.

flow.do: Ask your child to chew the rice slowly, without swallowing. Call out the time every 30 seconds. Ask what they taste each time. Write the answers down.
flow.say: Put the rice in your mouth. Chew slowly. I will tell you the time. What do you taste now? And now? Do not swallow yet.
flow.kid: Chew slowly. What do you taste now? And now?

ask.q: What did the rice taste like at the start, and after a minute?

flow.parent: Many people notice a sweet taste after about a minute. Some need two or three minutes. If nothing changes, keep chewing a little longer. Saliva needs time, and a little to work with.
flow.context: In this step, you chew the rice for two minutes and notice how the taste changes.

flow.do: Let your child swallow and rinse with water. Ask them to say what they thought, what they tasted and why.
flow.say: You can swallow now. Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you taste? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you tasted, and why.
flow.parent: After they have said what they tasted, explain: rice is mostly starch, which is long chains of glucose. Your saliva has an enzyme, a tool made by your cells, that cuts starch chains into short sugars. Short sugars taste sweet. This is the first step of digestion, and it breaks a polymer into small pieces.

check.q: Why does plain rice taste sweeter after long chewing?
options: Saliva cuts the starch chains into small sugars
The rice slowly turns into sugar by itself
Chewing squashes the sugar out of the rice
check.why: Starch is a long chain of glucose. An enzyme in saliva cuts it into short pieces that taste sweet. The rice does not change by itself, and chewing alone does not release sugar that was never there as small pieces.

flow.think: Where did the sweet taste come from, when we did not add any sugar?
flow.context: This is the last step of Chew the Rice. You explain what you found.

projects.title: Takli: spin your own cotton yarn

materials.item: a blunt pencil or a thin wooden stick about 20 centimetres long
an old CD, or a thick disc cut from card, about 8 centimetres wide with a hole in the middle
tape, and a paper clip to bend into a hook
a roll of cotton wool
a ruler

schedule.what: Spin a longer yarn and test it.

projects.record: Draw your takli. Measure your longest piece of yarn. Write what made it break, and what you would change.
projects.safety: Use a blunt pencil end. A grown-up helps with taping the disc.
projects.context: In this project, you make a takli, the spindle that Indian spinners have used for centuries, and spin your own yarn from cotton wool.

setup.art: A pencil pushed through the middle of an old CD with tape around it, and a bent paper clip taped at the top as a hook.
setup.caption: 1. Make the takli from a pencil, a disc and a paper clip hook.

setup.art: A hand spinning the takli like a top while it hangs from a thin wisp of cotton, with a growing yarn above it.
setup.caption: 2. Spin the takli like a top, and feed in cotton as it twists.

setup.art: A finished piece of yarn laid beside a ruler, with the takli resting on a table.
setup.caption: 3. Measure your yarn and compare it with a bought thread.

flow.do: Push a pencil through a hole in the middle of an old CD or a thick cardboard disc, 8 centimetres wide. Wrap tape around the pencil until the disc grips. Tape a bent paper clip to the top as a hook.
flow.say: A takli is a spindle. We make one today. The disc sits low on the stick. The hook sits at the top. The disc keeps the takli spinning.
flow.kid: Push a pencil through a disc. Tape a hook on top.
flow.parent: Use a blunt pencil end. A thick disc spins longer than a thin one. Hold the disc on with several turns of tape above and below it.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Takli project. You make a spindle that will twist cotton into yarn.

flow.do: Pull a long thin wisp from the cotton wool. Twist a short piece of it by hand, and loop it over the hook. Spin the takli like a top and let it hang. Feed more fibres with your other hand.
flow.say: Spin the takli like a top, and let it hang. The twist runs up into the wisp. Feed in a few more fibres with your other hand as it spins.
flow.kid: Spin the takli. Feed in fibres as it twists.

ask.q: What does the twist do to the loose cotton?

flow.parent: This takes practice. The first yarn is lumpy and breaks often. That is normal. A grown-up can spin a short piece first so the child can see. Keep the wisp thin and even. When the takli reaches the floor, wind the yarn onto the stick and start again.
flow.context: This is day 2 of the Takli project. You practise spinning your first yarn.

flow.do: Spin a longer yarn today. Then pull it between your hands and compare it with a loose wisp and a bought cotton thread. Measure the length of your yarn.
flow.say: Spin as much yarn as you can. Now pull your yarn gently. Compare it with a loose wisp and with a bought thread. What do you find?
flow.kid: Spin more yarn. Pull it gently. Compare it with bought thread.
flow.parent: Your yarn will be weaker than bought thread, and uneven. Machines and skilled spinners control the thickness and the twist very closely. After they have said what they see, explain: the twist makes the short fibres grip each other. This is how all cotton thread, and the thread in a sari, is made.

check.q: Which of these makes a stronger yarn?
options: Enough twist for the fibres to grip, but not so much that it kinks
As much twist as possible
No twist at all
check.why: Too little twist and the fibres slide apart. Too much and the yarn curls and fights itself. A good spinner finds the middle.

flow.think: Your yarn is longer than any fibre in it. What is holding it together?
flow.context: This is day 3 of the Takli project. You test your own yarn.

challenges.title: Newspaper Tower: hold the most books with four sheets of paper
challenges.problem: You have four sheets of newspaper and 40 centimetres of tape. Build a column exactly 25 centimetres tall. It must hold a stack of books on a flat tray for ten seconds. Hold as many books as you can.
constraints: Use only four sheets of newspaper and up to 40 centimetres of tape.
The column must be exactly 25 centimetres tall.
Books are added one at a time, gently, on a flat tray on top.
The column must hold for ten seconds to count.
Write down the number of books it held.
materials: a flat tray or a cardboard sheet
about 10 books or notebooks of the same size
general: Roll each sheet into a tube and tape it, so the tube has the paper's grain running along its length.
Join several tubes into a bundle and tape them together.
Make the tubes thin and tight, so they are stiffer than fat, loose tubes.
creative: Fold the paper into triangle-shaped tubes, which do not flatten as round ones do.
Put one tube inside another to make a wall twice as thick.
Tape tubes in a ring around an empty middle, like the legs of a table.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch your design. Build it and test it. Change one thing, such as how tight the tube is, and test again. Which design held the most books? Why do you think it did?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about the grain of paper. You build the strongest column you can from newspaper.

setup.art: A child sketching three column designs on paper: a single tube, a bundle of tubes and a triangle tube.
setup.caption: 1. Sketch some designs on paper.

setup.art: Two paper tubes standing side by side, each with an arrow along its length showing the paper's grain, one along and one across.
setup.caption: 2. Roll two tubes, one with the grain along the length and one across.

setup.art: A paper tube with a tray on top and a stack of books on the tray, and a count of books beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Add books one at a time and count them.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Ask your child to sketch two or three column designs, and to say which way the paper should be rolled, and why.
flow.say: You have four sheets of newspaper and a little tape. How could you make a column that holds the most books? Which way would you roll the paper? Draw some ideas first.
flow.kid: Draw two or three column ideas. Which way will you roll?

ask.q: What would make a paper column stronger?
good: Rolling it the way the fibres go.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Newspaper Tower challenge. You plan.

flow.do: Tear a strip from each of two sheets to find which way is straight. Roll one sheet so the straight direction runs along the length of the tube. Roll another the other way. Tape both, 25 centimetres tall.
flow.say: Find the straight-tearing direction on each sheet. Roll one tube with the straight direction along its length. Roll a second the other way. Tape them both, 25 centimetres tall.
flow.kid: Find the grain. Roll one tube with the grain along its length. Roll one the other way.
flow.parent: Roll tightly around a pencil, then pull the pencil out. Tape in three places. Both tubes must be the same width and height.
flow.context: In this step, you build two tubes that differ only in which way the paper is rolled.

flow.do: Stand one tube on the table. Put a flat tray on top. Add books one at a time, gently. Count the books when the tube bends or folds. Test the second tube the same way.
flow.say: Stand a tube up. Put a tray on top. Add the books one at a time, gently. Count how many it holds for ten seconds. Then test the other tube.
flow.kid: Stand a tube up. Add books one at a time. Count them.

check.q: Tube A holds 4 books and tube B holds 6 books. What can you say?
options: Tube B is stronger as built, but test again to be sure
Tube B is always stronger, whatever the paper
Tube A was not rolled
check.why: A bigger number is a clue. Repeat the test, since one try can be a fluke. Also check that the tubes are the same width and height.

flow.context: In this step, you load each tube and count how many books it holds.

flow.do: Now use all four sheets and 40 centimetres of tape to build your best column. Test it. Change one thing and test again.
flow.say: Use what you found. Build the strongest column you can from four sheets and 40 centimetres of tape. Test it. Then change one thing and test it again.
flow.kid: Build your best column. Test it. Change one thing. Test again.
flow.parent: Good ideas: several thin tubes taped side by side, a tube inside a tube, or a triangle shape. Change only one thing at a time.
flow.context: In this step, you use what you found to build your best column.

flow.do: Ask your child to say how many books their best column held, what made it strong, and why.
flow.say: How many books did your best column hold? What made it strong? Why do you think that worked?
flow.kid: How many books did it hold? Why did that work?
flow.parent: Paper is stiffer along its grain, so a tube with the grain along its length bends less. A difference between the tubes may be small. Write what you see.
flow.think: Which way would you roll if you were building a bridge from paper?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Newspaper Tower challenge. You explain your design.

challenges.title: Better Film: bendy but not sticky
challenges.problem: Using what you learned from the cornflour film test, make a film that folds at least ten times before it cracks, and is not sticky. The one thing you choose is the amount of glycerine.
constraints: Use 1 tablespoon of cornflour, 4 tablespoons of water and 1 teaspoon of vinegar.
Choose a glycerine amount between half a teaspoon and one and a half teaspoons.
Spread the film about the same size and thickness as the earlier films.
Let it dry for two to four days before testing.
materials: a small steel pan and a spoon
a steel plate and a few drops of oil
a ruler and a marker pen
general: Choose the amount that folded best in your first test.
Choose an amount halfway between the best two.
Choose a little less than the amount that felt sticky.
creative: Extra ideas, once your film works. Each one changes a second thing, so test it as a new film. Add a pinch of turmeric for colour, and see if it changes the bending.
Press a thread of cotton yarn into the wet film, like a strengthening wire.
Layer two thin films, one on top of the other, and test the pair.
challenges.your_turn: Choose your own glycerine amount. Cook and test your film. If you cook a second film, change only the glycerine again, and test it. Which film folded the most times and stayed unsticky? Why do you think it did?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You use your own earlier results to make a film that bends well and is not sticky.

setup.art: A child holding up their results chart from the cornflour film test, with a finger on the best bar.
setup.caption: 1. Look at your results and choose a glycerine amount.

setup.art: A small pan on a stove with clear thick gel, and a teaspoon of glycerine being stirred in.
setup.caption: 2. An adult cooks a small batch. Stir in your glycerine.

setup.art: A dry film on a plate, with a strip being folded in half and a count written beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Peel the dry film. Fold a strip and count the folds.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at the results of the Cornflour Film test. Ask your child to choose an amount of glycerine and say why.
flow.say: Look at your results from the cornflour films. Which amount made the best bending film without being sticky? What amount will you try? Why?
flow.kid: Look at your film results. Pick an amount of glycerine. Why?

ask.q: Which amount do you think is best, and why?
good: A little more than the best one.
Somewhere between two of the amounts.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Better Film challenge. You plan using your earlier results.

flow.do: Cook one new batch. Use 1 tablespoon of cornflour, 4 tablespoons of water and 1 teaspoon of vinegar. An adult heats it on low until it is clear and thick. Stir in your chosen glycerine. Spread it into a circle on an oiled plate.
flow.say: Cook a small batch of the same mix. An adult stirs it on low heat until it is clear and thick. Stir in your glycerine amount. Spread it thin on an oiled plate.
flow.kid: A grown-up cooks the mix. Stir in your glycerine. Spread it flat.
flow.parent: Choose a glycerine amount between half a teaspoon and one and a half teaspoons. Make the new film the same size and thickness as the earlier ones, so you can compare.
flow.context: In this step, you cook and spread your new film.

flow.do: Leave the plate on a flat shelf for two to four days.
flow.say: Leave the plate on a shelf. Check the day after tomorrow.
flow.kid: Leave the plate on a shelf for two to four days.
flow.context: In this step, you wait for the film to dry.

flow.do: Peel the film and cut a strip 2 centimetres wide. Fold and open it, and count the folds until it cracks. Stop at 20. Feel if it is sticky. Compare with your earlier films.
flow.say: Peel the film. Fold a strip, open it, and count. Is it sticky? How does it compare with your earlier films?
flow.kid: Peel the film. Fold a strip and count. Is it sticky?

check.q: Your new film folds 15 times and feels slightly sticky. Another film folds 14 times and is not sticky. Which is the better film for the job?
options: It depends on the job, so say what the job is
The one that folded 15 times, always
Neither, because both are sticky
check.why: A design has to meet the whole problem. Folding 15 times is slightly better, but the problem also asks for a film that is not sticky.

flow.context: In this step, you test your new film.

flow.do: Ask your child to say whether their new film solved the problem, and what they would change next.
flow.say: Did your film fold at least ten times and stay unsticky? Which glycerine amount worked best? What would you change next?
flow.kid: Did your film solve the problem? What would you change next?
flow.parent: Some films will not reach ten folds, and that is a good result to talk about. Films made in damp weather may stay sticky. Write exactly what you see.
flow.think: What would you add to the film to make it waterproof?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Better Film challenge. You judge your design.

schedule.what: Choose an amount, cook the film and spread it.
Peel the film, test it and judge it.
