quiz.p: Which of these describes a polymer best?
opts: A very long molecule made of many small pieces joined in a chain
A hard plastic made in a factory
A small molecule that dissolves in water
quiz.why: A polymer is any very long chain of repeating pieces. Cotton, hair and starch are polymers, as well as plastics. Not all polymers are plastic, and not all plastics are hard.

quiz.p: Rice and cotton are both chains of glucose. Why is cotton a tough fibre and rice soft food?
opts: Cellulose chains lie straight and hold each other tightly, while starch chains coil
Cotton has more glucose than rice
Rice is not made of chains
quiz.why: The same piece, joined in a slightly different way, gives chains of a different shape. Straight chains pack together side by side into tough fibres. Coiled chains do not.

quiz.p: A cotton thread is 500 metres long. Cotton fibres are about 2 centimetres long. What holds the thread together?
opts: The fibres overlap, and twist makes them grip each other
One very long fibre runs through the middle
A glue that cotton plants make
quiz.why: No fibre runs the whole length. Twist presses overlapping fibres together, so they grip. Untwist the thread, and it falls apart into short fibres.

quiz.p: Two strips are cut from one sheet of newspaper, one along the grain and one across it. Which holds more weight before it tears?
opts: The strip along the grain, because most fibres line up with the pull
The strip across the grain
They hold the same, since the paper is the same
quiz.why: Pulling along lined-up fibres pulls on the fibres themselves. Pulling across them only pulls on the weak holds between fibres.

quiz.p: A dry cornflour film cracks when you fold it. Which change would most likely help it bend?
opts: Adding some glycerine to the mix
Adding more cornflour
Drying it somewhere hotter
quiz.why: Glycerine sits between the starch chains and lets them slide. More cornflour makes the film thicker and still stiff. Hotter drying can make a film curl or crack.

quiz.p: A handle on a pan must not soften on the stove. Which kind of plastic is best for it?
opts: A thermoset, because its chains are tied together all through
A thermoplastic like a carry bag, because it bends easily
Any plastic, because heat never changes plastic
quiz.why: Ties between chains hold a thermoset firm in heat. A thermoplastic softens when heated, because its chains slide.

quiz.p: If two tries of the same test give very different numbers, you should repeat the test a few more times before trusting either number.
quiz.why: True. One try can be a fluke. Several tries show the pattern, and how much the results vary.

quiz.p: Why is nylon thread stretched in the factory after it is spun?
opts: Stretching lines up the chains, so the thread is stronger along its length
Stretching makes the chains shorter
Stretching makes the nylon melt
quiz.why: In the factory, pulling a thread straightens and lines up its chains. Lined-up chains share a pull better, so the thread holds more.

quiz.p: A curl of hair gets straighter when it is wet. What does the water do?
opts: It gets between the chains and loosens the ties that hold the curl
It makes new chains in the hair
It melts the hair
quiz.why: Water loosens the weak ties between protein chains. The chains slide into a new shape. When the hair dries, the ties form again and hold the shape.

quiz.p: Which of these is not a polymer?
opts: Table salt
Silk
Rice starch
quiz.why: Silk is a protein chain. Starch is a glucose chain. Salt is a crystal of two kinds of atom, with no long chains of repeating molecules.

quiz.p: Why can an old PET bottle be melted and made into something new?
opts: It is a thermoplastic, so its chains slide when heated and set again when cooled
It is a thermoset, so it melts completely
It has no chains in it
quiz.why: Heat lets thermoplastic chains slide past each other, so the plastic can be reshaped. A thermoset's chains are tied together and cannot slide.

quiz.p: A rope breaks where it has been rubbed smooth against a stone for months. What most likely happened there?
opts: The rubbing loosened the twist, so the fibres slid out
The stone cut every fibre in half
The fibres there were always weaker
quiz.why: A rope holds because twist makes its fibres grip. Rubbing loosens the twist, so the fibres can slide, and the rope fails at that place.

items.p: What does the word monomer mean?
opts: One small piece that can join with others in a chain
Another word for plastic
A very long chain of many pieces
items.why: Mono means one. A monomer is one small piece. Many monomers joined in a chain make a polymer.

items.p: Human hair and a plastic carry bag are both polymers.
items.why: True. Hair is a protein chain that your body makes. Polythene is a chain of ethylene pieces joined in a factory. Both are very long chains of small pieces.

items.p: A very long molecule made of many small pieces joined together is called a ____.
items.why: Poly means many. A polymer is many pieces joined in a chain.

items.p: Match each polymer to what makes it.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Cotton plants and silkworms build their polymers in their own bodies. Factories join ethylene pieces to make polythene. Your body builds hair from food.

items.p: Sort each polymer by who made it.
items.a: as given
items.why: Wool, starch and the cellulose in paper are built by living things. Nylon, PET and polystyrene foam are built in factories from chemicals, mostly from oil and gas.

items.p: Why does a sheet of newspaper tear straight in one direction?
opts: Most of its fibres line up in that direction
It is thicker in that direction
It is wetter in that direction
items.why: A tear runs easily between lined-up fibres. Across them, it must break fibres, so it wanders.

items.p: A cotton thread is 400 metres long. One cotton fibre is 2 centimetres long. If the fibres lay end to end with no overlap, how many fibres would the thread need?
items.why: 400 metres is 40,000 centimetres. 40,000 divided by 2 is 20,000. A real thread needs far more fibres than this, because the fibres overlap.

items.p: Maya says: 'A thread can never be longer than its longest fibre.' Explain why she is wrong.
items.a: A cotton fibre is only two or three centimetres long, but a cotton thread can be hundreds of metres long. The fibres overlap, and twisting makes them grip each other, so the thread holds together.
items.why: A strong answer says that the fibres overlap and that twist makes them grip, and uses a measurement such as the length of a fibre and the length of a thread.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Cotton, silk, steel, wool.
items.a: Steel, because it is a metal. The others are polymers.
items.why: Cotton is cellulose, silk and wool are proteins. Steel is metal atoms packed together, not chains.

items.p: A dry strip of starch film cracks when folded. A few drops of glycerine go into a new batch. What is the best prediction?
opts: The new film bends more, because glycerine sits between the chains and lets them slide
The new film is stiffer, because glycerine is thick
The new film is the same, because glycerine is only a liquid
items.why: A plasticiser is a small molecule that sits between chains and keeps them a little apart. The chains can then slide, and the film bends.

items.p: A thermoset can be melted and moulded again, just like a thermoplastic.
items.why: False. A thermoset has chains tied to each other in many places. Heat cannot make them slide, so it chars instead of melting.

items.p: Draw a close-up of a sheet of newspaper showing its fibres. Add an arrow along the direction it tears straight.
items.a: Many short lines, mostly lying in one direction, and an arrow pointing the same way.
items.why: A strong drawing shows most fibres lined up, and the arrow in the direction of the lined-up fibres.

items.p: Lakshmi and Farhan are choosing a shirt for hot, rainy Chennai days.

views.who: Lakshmi, a girl in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: A cotton shirt is better. Cotton grows on a plant, and the cloth breathes.

views.who: Farhan, a boy in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: A polyester shirt is better. It dries fast and lasts long, and growing cotton needs a lot of water.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with more? What would you want to find out to be sure?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side, gives a reason, and says what to test or look up, such as how fast each dries or how much water each needs.
items.why: Both have a point. A made material is not good or bad because of where it came from. It depends on what it is used for, and on what it costs to make.

items.p: Starch and cellulose are both made of the same sugar, called ____.
items.why: Both are chains of glucose. They are joined in different ways, so starch coils and cellulose lies straight.

items.p: A girl tests two films, but the amount of glycerine, the thickness and the drying time are all different. What is wrong with her test?
opts: Many things changed at once, so she cannot tell which one caused the difference
Nothing is wrong, since more differences give more information
She should have used only one film
items.why: A fair test changes one thing. If three things change, any difference could be from any of them.

items.p: Name two polymers that living beings make, and two that people make in factories.
items.a: Living beings make cotton, silk, wool, hair, starch or rubber. People make polythene, PET, nylon or polystyrene.
items.why: Any two from each group are right. Living beings build cellulose, protein and starch. Factories build plastics from oil or gas.

items.p: Put these in the right order, for what happens when you chew a piece of rice for a long time.
a: You chew rice, which is made of long starch chains
An enzyme in your saliva cuts the starch chains at their joins
items.why: Starch is a long chain of glucose. An enzyme in saliva cuts the chains into short sugars. Short sugars taste sweet.

items.p: A strip cut from a plastic bottle shrinks in very hot water. What is the best reason?
opts: The chains were pulled straight when the bottle was made, and heat lets them coil up again
Heat makes some of the plastic evaporate
Heat makes new chains join the strip
items.why: Bottle walls are stretched when they are made, so their chains are lined up. In hot water the chains wiggle and coil, and the strip shrinks.

items.p: Stretching a nylon thread in the factory can make it stronger along its length.
items.why: True. Stretching lines up the chains, and lined-up chains share a pull well.

items.p: Match each thing to what describes it best.
pairs: thermoplastic, can be melted and reshaped
chains tied together at a few places
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: A cooker handle must not soften, so its chains are tied everywhere. A bottle can be melted and reshaped. Tyre rubber has a few ties that keep it stretchy. Cotton is cellulose.

items.p: These made-up results are for three cornflour films. The best film folded how many more times than the worst film?

chart.title: Made-up results: folds before a cornflour film cracked

items.why: The best film folded 14 times and the worst folded 2 times. 14 take away 2 is 12.

items.p: A strip of plastic is 8 centimetres long. After hot water it is 6 centimetres long. By how many centimetres did it shrink?
items.why: 8 take away 6 is 2. The strip shrank by 2 centimetres, which is one quarter of its length.

items.p: Sort each plastic thing by whether it softens in heat or stays firm.
items.a: as given
items.why: Bottles, bags and polystyrene soften because their chains are free to slide. Handles, melamine plates and Bakelite are thermosets, with chains tied to each other.

items.p: A coir rope snapped at the place where it had rubbed on a stone all season, and not where it was new. Explain why, using the words fibre and twist.
items.a: The rubbing wore the twist loose at that place. Loose twist means the fibres no longer grip each other, so they slide out when the rope is pulled.
items.why: A strong answer says the rope fails where the twist is loose, because twist is what makes the short fibres grip.

items.p: Asha and Imran are arguing about a rope.

views.who: Asha, a girl in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: A rope is one thing. It holds a boat as one piece.

views.who: Imran, a boy in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: A rope is many things. Take it apart and you only have fibres.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with more? What would count as evidence for your side?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason, such as that the rope acts as one piece when pulled, or that untwisting it leaves only loose fibres.
items.why: Both have a point. The rope does act as one piece, and it is also made of many fibres. It depends on what you are asking.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Rice, potato, chapati dough, cotton thread.
items.a: Cotton thread, because it is made of cellulose. The others are mostly starch.
items.why: Rice, potato and wheat flour are rich in starch. Cotton is mostly cellulose. Both are glucose chains, but they are joined differently.

items.p: An enzyme that cuts starch cannot cut cellulose. What does this tell us?
opts: The joins between glucose pieces are different, so one tool does not fit both
Cellulose is not made of glucose
Starch has no chains
items.why: Both are glucose chains, but the joins have different shapes. An enzyme fits one kind of join, like a key fits one lock.

items.p: Silk needs much less twist than cotton to hold together, because a silkworm makes one fibre hundreds of metres long.
items.why: True. A fibre that is already very long does not need twist to hold it. Short fibres, like cotton and wool, need twist to grip.

items.p: A material made of lined-up fibres is strongest along the ____ of the fibres, and weakest across them.
items.why: Pulling along the fibres pulls on the fibres themselves, which is strong. Pulling across them pulls only on the weak holds between them.

items.p: Draw two pairs of chains. In one pair, the chains are pressed tight together. In the other, small dots sit between the chains. Label which pair is a stiff film and which is a bendy film.
items.a: Tight chains labelled stiff. Chains with dots between them labelled bendy.
items.why: A plasticiser sits between chains and keeps them apart, so they can slide. Chains pressed tight together hold each other and the film is stiff.

items.p: A girl folds one strip of film and it cracks. She says the film is brittle. What should she do before she decides?
opts: Test a few more strips from the same film
Say her answer is final
Throw the film away
items.why: One strip can be a fluke, for example if it had a crack or a thin place. More tries show whether the film really is brittle.

items.p: Explain, in terms of chains, why a pressure cooker handle is a thermoset and a PET bottle is a thermoplastic.
items.a: A thermoset has chains tied to each other in many places, so heat cannot make them slide, and it does not melt. A thermoplastic has chains that are free to slide when heated, so it softens and can be reshaped.
items.why: A strong answer mentions ties between chains for the handle and chains free to slide for the bottle.

items.p: The stiff chains of Kevlar line up side by side before the fibre is spun. Why does that make a very strong fibre?
opts: When the fibre is pulled, the pull runs along the strong bonds of the chains and not across weak holds
Stiff chains are heavier, so they are stronger
Liquids always make strong fibres
items.why: A pull along a chain pulls on strong bonds between atoms. A fibre whose chains all lie along its length uses those strong bonds for the whole pull.

items.p: A garden hose and a water pipe are both PVC. The hose is soft and the pipe is stiff. What most likely explains this?
opts: The hose has a plasticiser between its chains, so they slide
The pipe has shorter chains
The hose is not a polymer
items.why: A plasticiser keeps chains a little apart and lets them slide. Without it, the same chains stay stiff.

items.p: A takli spinner makes 2 metres of yarn in 10 minutes. At the same rate, how many minutes will it take to spin 10 metres?
items.why: 10 metres is 5 times 2 metres. So the time is 5 times 10 minutes, which is 50 minutes.

items.p: Some made-up results: 0 teaspoons of glycerine gave 2 folds, 1 teaspoon gave 14 folds, and 2 teaspoons gave 9 folds. Someone says 'more glycerine always means more folds.' Do the numbers agree? Explain.
items.a: No. 2 teaspoons gave fewer folds than 1 teaspoon. A little glycerine helps a lot, but too much makes the film soft, and it tears.
items.why: A strong answer uses the numbers to show the claim fails, and gives a reason such as too much glycerine making the film weak.

chart.title: Made-up results: folds before a cornflour film cracked

items.p: Put these in the right order, for what happens to a stretched bottle strip in hot water.
a: Heat is added to the strip
Stretched, lined-up chains coil up again
items.why: Heat gives the chains energy to move. Chains that were pulled straight when the bottle was made now coil up, so the strip shrinks.

items.p: Old PET bottles can be recycled by melting them, because PET is a thermoplastic.
items.why: True. A thermoplastic softens in heat and sets again when it cools, so it can be reshaped.

items.p: Sort each by what its chains are made of.
items.a: as given
items.why: Hair and silk are proteins, which are chains of amino acids. Cotton and rice are chains of glucose. Salt and water are made of small units, not long chains.

items.p: Two children look at a cooker handle that is a net of strong ties right through.

views.who: Neha, a girl in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: It is one giant molecule, because every atom is joined to the others.

views.who: Karan, a boy in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: It is not one molecule. A molecule is a group of atoms of a set size, and this has no set size.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with more? What does the word molecule mean to you?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side and says what they think counts as one thing.
items.why: Chemists really do disagree. The question is about what we mean by the word molecule, and a good answer says what the word means to them.

items.p: A factory stretches a newly spun nylon thread. Explain what happens to the chains, and why the thread gets stronger.
items.a: Stretching pulls the chains straight and lines them up along the thread. Lined-up chains share a pull along their strong bonds, so the thread holds more.
items.why: A strong answer says the chains line up along the thread and use their strong bonds for the pull.

items.p: A child wants to find out whether more twist makes cotton thread hold more. Which is a fair test?
opts: Same cotton, same length, change only the number of twists, and repeat each
Use a different kind of cotton for each thread
Twist one thread and use a longer one with no twist
items.why: Only the twist should change. Everything else, such as cotton and length, stays the same. Repeating each test shows whether the result is steady.

items.p: Three of these loosen the holds between chains. Which is the odd one out? Adding glycerine to starch, wetting a curl of hair, warming a plastic, stretching nylon in a factory.
items.a: Stretching nylon in a factory, because it lines up the chains and makes them hold more. The others loosen the holds between chains.
items.why: Glycerine, water and heat loosen the holds between chains, so the material bends or softens. Stretching lines the chains up so they hold each other better.

items.p: Draw a close-up of a cotton yarn: four short fibres overlapping, with the twist drawn as a spiral. Mark where one fibre ends and the next begins.
items.a: Four short fibres overlapping along a spiral, with the end points marked.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that no one fibre runs the whole way, and that the fibres overlap and the twist wraps around them.

items.p: Match each material to the main polymer in it.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Rice is mostly starch. Egg white is mostly protein. Cotton is cellulose. The sap of a rubber tree holds rubber chains.

items.p: A cooker handle is a net of strong ties right through the plastic. Give your view: is it one molecule or many? Give a reason.
items.a: Answers vary. One view: it is one giant molecule, because all its atoms are joined by strong bonds. Another view: it is not, because a molecule has a set size and this does not.
items.why: A strong answer takes a side, gives a reason, and says what counts as one molecule.

items.p: A takli, a charkha and a coir wheel all do the same job. What is it?
opts: They twist short fibres into a long yarn
They melt fibres into plastic
They cut long fibres into short ones
items.why: Spinning twists fibres together so they grip. It turns short fibres into a long yarn.

items.p: A small molecule that sits between polymer chains and lets them slide is called a ____.
items.why: A plasticiser keeps the chains a little apart. Glycerine is a plasticiser for starch.

open_questions.q: Can we make plastics that mend their own scratches and cracks?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have made polymers that mend themselves in the lab, but most do not yet last long enough or cost little enough to be used every day.

open_questions.q: How do wood, bone and tendon line up their chains so well, and can people copy it?
open_questions.why_open: Living things build strong materials at room temperature from water and simple foods. Factories still need heat and oil to make anything as strong.

open_questions.q: How much plastic is in the sea, and where does it go over time?
open_questions.why_open: Plastic has existed for only about a hundred years. Estimates of how much is in the sea differ a lot, and nobody has followed a piece for its whole life.

open_questions.q: Is a thermoset such as a cooker handle one giant molecule?
open_questions.why_open: The answer depends on what we mean by a molecule, and chemists do not all agree on that.

maths.problem: In the Wisp and Thread activity, a child found that one cotton fibre was 2 centimetres long. A thread is 5 metres long. If the fibres lay end to end with no overlap, how many would the thread need? Would a real thread need more or fewer, and why?
maths.answer: 250 fibres. A real thread needs more.
maths.explain: 5 metres is 500 centimetres. 500 divided by 2 is 250. Real fibres overlap, so many more are needed to cover the same length.
maths.context: In the Wisp and Thread activity, you pull one fibre out of a twisted thread and measure it.
maths.why_maths: Counting how many short fibres make a long thread shows that no single fibre can run the whole way.

maths.problem: These are made-up results from three cornflour films. The best film folded how many times as many as the worst film? Which film would you choose for a bag, and why?

chart.title: Made-up results: folds before a cornflour film cracked

maths.answer: 7 times as many. The 1 teaspoon film.
maths.explain: 14 divided by 2 is 7. The best film folded 7 times as many as the worst. The film with 1 teaspoon bends the most and is probably not too sticky, but you would test it.
maths.context: In the Cornflour Film test, you fold each film until it cracks and count the folds.
maths.why_maths: A ratio tells us how many times better one result is than another, which is easier to judge than two separate numbers.

maths.problem: The recipe for three films uses 3 tablespoons of cornflour and 12 tablespoons of water. A class wants to make 12 films from the same recipe. How many tablespoons of cornflour and of water do they need?
maths.answer: 12 tablespoons of cornflour and 48 tablespoons of water.
maths.explain: 12 films is 4 times as many as 3 films. 3 times 4 is 12 tablespoons of cornflour. 12 times 4 is 48 tablespoons of water.
maths.context: In the Cornflour Film test, one pot of mix makes three films.
maths.why_maths: Scaling a recipe keeps the amounts in the same proportion, so the films come out the same.

maths.problem: Imagine two made-up results from a Hot Water test. One strip was 8 centimetres long and shrank to 6 centimetres. A longer strip was 10 centimetres long and shrank to 5 centimetres. What fraction of its length did each strip lose? Which shrank by the bigger fraction?
maths.answer: The first lost one quarter. The second lost one half. The second shrank by the bigger fraction.
maths.explain: The first lost 2 centimetres out of 8, which is 2 over 8, or one quarter. The second lost 5 out of 10, which is one half. One half is bigger than one quarter.
maths.context: In the Hot Water test, you measure each plastic strip before and after it sits in hot water.
maths.why_maths: Comparing fractions of the starting length is fair, because the strips did not start at the same length.

maths.problem: In the Wisp and Thread activity, a child spun a pencil 30 times for a thread 10 centimetres long. How many turns is that for each centimetre? If the thread is 25 centimetres long, how many turns would give the same twist?
maths.explain: 30 divided by 10 is 3 turns for each centimetre. 25 centimetres times 3 turns is 75 turns. Turns for each centimetre is a fair way to compare twist.
maths.context: In the Wisp and Thread activity, you count the turns of a pencil to twist a wisp into a thread.
maths.why_maths: Twist depends on the length of the thread, so turns for each centimetre is a fair measure that lets us compare threads of different lengths.

roots.context: We have torn, twisted, cooked and heated polymers. Now we ask what a thread made of short pieces tells us about wholes, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: A cotton thread is far longer than any cotton fibre in it. Twisted, short fibres grip each other and hold a load together. So the thread's strength is not in any one fibre, but in the way many pieces hold each other.
deep_truth.habit: We picture a long, strong thing as one long, strong piece, like a rod. A thread, a rope and a sheet of paper are not like that, even though they look like one piece.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Wisp and Thread activity, a loose wisp of cotton came apart in your fingers. The same cotton, twisted, held together as a thread. A single fibre from it was only a centimetre or two long.

three.who_am_i: Your hair, nails and skin are made of protein chains that your body joined from the food you ate. You are made of short pieces that hold on to each other, just as a thread is.
three.what_is_life: Every cell joins amino acids into protein chains, one piece at a time, in the order written in the genes. Making long chains out of short pieces is part of what living things do.
three.what_is_this_world: Rope, cloth, paper, wood and bone are all long, strong things made of short pieces holding on. At every size, from chains to fibres to yarn to rope, the holding is done by pieces that are short.

roots.thread: A cotton plant grows short fibres. A spinner twists many of them into a thread much longer than any one fibre, and a weaver crosses threads into cloth. At each step, nothing new is added. The same small pieces are held together in a new way. What they can do together is more than any one of them could do alone.

teachings.teaching: The thinker Gargi asks Yajnavalkya what the world is woven on, as a cloth is woven from warp and weft. He answers step by step, and each answer is woven on the next.
teachings.link: The Upanishad pictures the world as woven cloth, and asks what the cloth rests on. A thread gives a plain, physical answer to a similar question: each fibre is held by its neighbours, with nothing else holding the whole thread up.

teachings.source: Kabir, the poem Jhini Jhini Bini Chadariya (traditionally about the 15th century, Varanasi)
teachings.teaching: Kabir is remembered as a weaver. In this poem he sings of the body as a fine cloth woven on a loom, and asks who wove it.
teachings.link: Kabir used the work of his own hands to ask about life. A cloth is short fibres twisted into thread and crossed into cloth, and a body is made of small parts held together too.

science.text: Materials are built in layers. Chains pack into fibrils, fibrils into fibres, fibres into yarn, and yarn into cloth. Wood and bone are built this way too, and strength comes from every layer.
Living things build strong materials from simple foods at room temperature. Scientists would like to design materials that build themselves in the same way, but this is still far from done.

other_view.who: Nagasena, a Buddhist teacher, in the Milindapanha (The Questions of King Milinda)
other_view.view: A chariot is only a name for its wheels, axle, frame and pole put together. There is no chariot apart from the parts. In the same way, a thread is only a name for fibres with a twist, and there is nothing more to find.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1965, Stephanie Kwolek was a chemist at a company called DuPont in the United States. She was looking for a very light, very strong fibre that could be used inside car tyres. She made a new polymer with very stiff chains and dissolved it. Chemists expected a thick, clear syrup. Hers was thin, cloudy and runny, and most chemists would have thrown it away. She asked a technician to spin it into a fibre. By most accounts, he was unsure the cloudy liquid would work in his machine, but he agreed. The fibre was stiff and very strong. She tested it again and again, because she could hardly believe the numbers. The cloud was a sign that the stiff chains had lined up side by side in the liquid. Spun into a fibre, the lined-up chains made a fibre stronger than steel for the same weight. This fibre is called Kevlar.
how_we_found_out.who: Stephanie Kwolek, a chemist at DuPont, with Paul Morgan, who worked with her on making the polymer, and Charles Smullen, the technician who spun it
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Chemists thought that a good polymer solution should be clear and thick, and that a cloudy, runny one was a failure. Kwolek spun the cloudy liquid anyway and showed that the cloud was a sign of lined-up chains, which make a very strong fibre.
